Phase 1 -- system map: document the analyzed service's components, external
dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
I'll start by loading the tool schemas and exploring the codebase.

Read the whole service. It's a small Python key-value store: one public read entrypoint, an in-memory cache, a flat-file store, a background evictor, and an internal write path. Proposing the map now.

payload_or_id.name: get_value read entrypoint (kvstore/api.py)
payload_or_id.description: The only client-facing operation the service exposes: get_value(cache, key). Delegates the read to Cache and returns whatever Cache hands back. Wraps the call in a try/except for StorageError, incrementing kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} and re-raising on failure, and {outcome="success"} otherwise. This counter is the service's only instrumentation. It counts call outcomes only: a cache hit returns the cached value without consulting storage, so a served-but-stale or served-but-wrong value is counted as a success and is indistinguishable from a correct one at this boundary.

payload_or_id.name: In-memory cache (kvstore/cache.py)
payload_or_id.description: Unbounded in-process dict of key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms) sitting in front of Storage. get(key) consults its own dict first and returns the cached value if present; on a miss it reads through to Storage and inserts the result, stamping inserted_at_ms with time.time() * 1000 (milliseconds). It never re-checks Storage for an already-cached key and never expires anything itself. It caches negative results too: a Storage miss returns None, which is stored as an Entry and returned on every later read of that key. items() exposes all entries for the evictor to walk; evict(key) removes one entry and is the only removal path. There is no size limit, no entry count, and no hit/miss instrumentation.

payload_or_id.name: Flat-file backing store (kvstore/storage.py)
payload_or_id.description: Persists all key-value pairs to a single delimited text file, one "key,value" line per pair. get(key) returns None if the file is absent, otherwise reads the whole file and linear-scans it, splitting each line on the first comma and returning the first matching key. put(key, value) reads the entire file into a dict, sets the key, creates the parent directory, and rewrites the whole file in one write_text call. Both operations are whole-file, so cost grows linearly with the number of stored keys, and put is a full-file rewrite with no atomic rename or locking. OSError from any read or write is wrapped in StorageError and raised to the caller; no other failure (a key whose value contains a comma, a key containing a comma, a truncated file) raises or is otherwise signalled. Not instrumented.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file and its filesystem
payload_or_id.description: The single flat file on local disk that Storage reads and rewrites, together with the filesystem holding it. Its path is injected into Storage at construction; nothing in this repo creates, sizes, backs up, or checks it. It is shared mutable state between the read path (via cache misses) and the write path (admin.update_value), with no locking, so a concurrent reader can observe a partially rewritten file. Failures the service can see through it: missing or unreadable file, permission denial, disk full or read-only mount on write, and I/O errors -- all surfacing as OSError and therefore StorageError. Failures it cannot see: silent corruption and content lost by an interrupted full-file rewrite.

payload_or_id.name: TTL eviction pass (kvstore/evictor.py)
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass(cache) walks every cache entry, collects the keys it judges older than TTL_SECONDS (300), evicts each, and returns the count removed so a caller could log or observe progress. This is the only mechanism bounding cache size and the only mechanism that ever lets a stale cache entry be re-read from storage. Its expiry comparison is broken as written: it compares now = time.time() (seconds) against entry.inserted_at_ms (milliseconds), so now - inserted_at_ms is a large negative number that never exceeds TTL_SECONDS. The predicate is never true, the pass always evicts zero entries and returns 0, and both of the guarantees resting on it are silently absent. The return value is currently discarded -- nothing in this repo consumes or records it.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction scheduler loop (assumed, not in this repo)
payload_or_id.description: The periodic caller that is meant to invoke run_eviction_pass on a schedule. Referenced by evictor.py's docstring ("a caller (e.g. a scheduler loop)") and by the README, but no code in this repo constructs, schedules, or invokes it -- so its interval, its process, and whether it runs at all are unverified assumptions of this analysis, and it is a live possibility that eviction is never invoked in a deployment. Recorded as a distinct component because it fails independently of the pass itself: a scheduler that stops, wedges, or was never wired up produces unbounded cache growth and permanently stale reads just as the broken predicate inside the pass does, and neither is currently distinguishable from the other or from healthy operation.

payload_or_id.name: Internal write path (kvstore/admin.py)
payload_or_id.description: update_value(storage, cache, key, value) is the service's write path, internal and not reachable by external clients. It calls storage.put and nothing else. It takes a Cache argument and never uses it: cache.evict(key) exists for exactly this purpose and is not called, so a key already resident in the cache keeps serving its pre-write value to readers indefinitely -- the write is durable in storage yet invisible through the read path. Recovery depends entirely on the evictor, which never expires anything. StorageError from put propagates to the caller; the function has no instrumentation, so neither a successful write nor a failed one is counted.

payload_or_id.name: Periodic data-sync job (assumed, not in this repo)
payload_or_id.description: The periodic caller that drives update_value to refresh stored data, described in admin.py's docstring and the README as the reason the write path exists. No code in this repo schedules or invokes it, so its cadence and its error handling are unverified assumptions. It is the sole known writer, which makes it the origin of every stale-read chain: whether it succeeded, failed, or has not run since some past time is not recorded anywhere in the service, so a sync that silently stops leaves readers served indefinitely from cache and storage with no signal distinguishing it from a healthy, quiet system.

payload_or_id.name: prometheus_client instrumentation and its scrape path
payload_or_id.description: prometheus_client 0.26.0 (the service's only third-party dependency, pinned in requirements.txt) provides the single Counter kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}, defined at import time in api.py against the library's default registry. This is the entire observability surface every phase-4 alert must ultimately be built on, so its own availability is load-bearing. Nothing in this repo exposes the registry: there is no HTTP metrics endpoint, no start_http_server call, and no push gateway, so how these counts reach a scraper is defined outside this repo and is an unverified assumption of this analysis. Until that path is confirmed, an unconfigured or unscraped registry is indistinguishable from a service reporting no traffic.

event.text:
Phase 1 accepted — 9 components proposed.

**The service:** a minimal Python key-value store, ~120 lines, one third-party dependency (`prometheus_client==0.26.0`).

**Read path (client-facing):** `sm-api-get-value` → `sm-cache` → `sm-storage` → `sm-storage-file`
**Write path (internal):** `sm-data-sync-job` → `sm-admin-update-value` → `sm-storage`
**Maintenance:** `sm-evictor-scheduler` → `sm-evictor` → `sm-cache`

Three things worth flagging now, because they shape phases 2–4:

1. **The read and write paths only meet at the file.** `admin.update_value` receives a `Cache` and never touches it, though `cache.evict()` exists for exactly that purpose. So a durable write is invisible to readers whose key is already cached — the write succeeds and the read stays wrong.

2. **The one mechanism that would recover from that is inert.** `run_eviction_pass` compares `time.time()` (seconds) against `Entry.inserted_at_ms` (milliseconds); the difference is always large and negative, so nothing is ever evicted. That single defect breaks *both* guarantees resting on it — cache boundedness and eventual staleness recovery — and the pass returns 0 either way, which is also what a healthy idle pass returns.

3. **Two components are assumptions, not code.** Neither the eviction scheduler nor the data-sync job exists in this repo — both are named only in docstrings and the README. I recorded them as components anyway, because they fail independently of the code they'd call, and a scheduler that was never wired up is currently indistinguishable from the broken predicate above. Similarly, nothing exposes the Prometheus registry (no `start_http_server`, no push gateway), so the path by which the one existing metric reaches a scraper is undefined here. If you can tell me how these three are actually deployed, that materially changes what phase 4 can recommend; otherwise I'll carry them as explicit unverified assumptions.

The overall shape for phase 2: the only instrumentation is a counter of call outcomes at the entrypoint, and every defect above produces a *successful* call returning a wrong value. The failure chains are real; the visible ends mostly aren't.

Ready for phase 2 (failure modes) when you are.

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction expiry predicate compares seconds against milliseconds
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes now = time.time() (seconds since epoch, ~1.7e9) and tests now - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS, where inserted_at_ms was stamped as time.time() * 1000 (~1.7e12). The difference is approximately -1.7e12, never greater than 300, for every entry regardless of age. This is the root defect of two otherwise independent chains -- cache boundedness and staleness recovery -- which is why it is documented separately from either. Deterministic and present on every pass since the code was written; it is a code defect to be fixed under a ticket rather than a condition an operator can resolve at 3am, hence warning rather than critical despite the severity of what it causes downstream.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass completes successfully having removed no entries
payload_or_id.description: Every invocation of run_eviction_pass walks the full cache, matches no entry, evicts nothing, and returns 0 -- reporting success. This is the single load-bearing link: it is simultaneously the reason the cache is unbounded and the reason a stale entry is never re-read from storage. It has two distinct upstream causes that produce an identical observable state (zero evictions), namely the unit mismatch in the predicate and the scheduler never invoking the pass at all; nothing currently distinguishes them, or distinguishes either from a genuinely idle cache in which no entry has yet aged out. The return value that would carry this signal is discarded by every caller.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction scheduler never invokes the pass
payload_or_id.description: No code in this repo schedules run_eviction_pass, so the pass runs only if something outside the repo calls it. The failure covers three cases with the same effect: the scheduler was never wired up, its process died, or its loop is wedged or backed off. Independent of the predicate defect -- fixing the units leaves this failure fully intact, and it would then be the sole remaining reason the cache is never trimmed. Distinguishing 'the pass ran and found nothing' from 'the pass never ran' requires a signal emitted by the pass itself, which does not currently exist.

payload_or_id.name: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache._entries only ever gains keys. Insertion happens on every miss, including misses that resolve to None, and the sole removal path is Cache.evict, which is called only by an eviction pass that removes nothing. Under sustained unique-key traffic the dict grows monotonically for the lifetime of the process, bounded only by available memory. Warning rather than critical because it degrades over hours or days rather than instantly, leaving time to act -- but only if something is watching, and no entry count is exported today.

payload_or_id.name: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value accepts a Cache parameter and never touches it. Cache.evict exists for precisely this call and is not made, so after a successful, durable write to storage the cache continues to hold and serve the pre-write value for that key. The write is not lost -- it is invisible. Critical because the resulting divergence between storage and cache is permanent for the process lifetime: with eviction inert there is no path back to consistency short of a restart, and no error is raised at any point in either the write or the subsequent reads.

payload_or_id.name: Absent key is cached as None and never re-checked
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a storage miss as Entry(value=None) and returns the cached None on every subsequent read. Because get tests entry is not None rather than testing membership, a cached None is a hit and never reads through. Any key read before it is first written is therefore pinned to None for the process lifetime even after the writer populates it -- turning a transient absence, or a read that raced ahead of the data-sync job, into a permanent one. Distinct from the write-invalidation gap: this one poisons on a read, and needs no write to have occurred at all.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file missing, so every key reads as absent
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get checks self._path.exists() and returns None when the file is gone, treating a vanished store as an empty one. Deletion, a wrong or unmounted path, an empty volume after a redeploy, and a fresh host that never received the data all present identically, and none raises. Because the miss then reads through into the cache as a cached None, a file absent for even a moment can pin keys to None long after the file returns.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file read raises OSError
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get wraps its read in try/except OSError and raises StorageError. Covers permission denial, an I/O error, a disappeared mount, and a descriptor or memory limit hit while reading the whole file. Unlike the absent-file case this one is loud: it is the single failure the existing instrumentation can already see, because it propagates through get_value and increments the error-labelled counter.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file write raises OSError
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put wraps read, mkdir, and write_text in try/except OSError and raises StorageError to its caller. Covers a full disk, a read-only or remounted filesystem, permission denial, and a quota breach. The caller is the data-sync job, outside this repo and outside the read path's instrumentation, so a write path that is failing every attempt produces no signal anywhere in this service. Readers see no error at all -- they see data that has quietly stopped changing.

payload_or_id.name: put rewrites the whole file in place with no atomicity or locking
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads every pair into a dict, then calls write_text, which truncates the file and writes the new contents. There is no temp-file-plus-rename, no lock, and no fsync. Two consequences follow, both silent: a reader whose read_text lands inside that window observes a truncated or partial file, and a crash, kill, container eviction, or disk-full condition mid-write leaves the file permanently truncated. Every key in the store is at risk on every single write, because each write rewrites all of them.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two overlapping writers each read the same starting contents and each rewrite the whole file; the later write wins wholesale, discarding not only the other writer's key but any key written between its own read and its write. Both writers return successfully. Only reachable with more than one concurrent writer -- with a single serial data-sync job it cannot occur -- so it is recorded as warning and as conditional on a deployment fact this analysis has not verified.

payload_or_id.name: Unescaped comma delimiter collides keys and truncates values
payload_or_id.description: Both get and put split each line on the first comma with str.partition and neither escapes nor validates the delimiter. A key containing a comma is therefore unreachable and collides with another key: put("a,b", "c") writes the line "a,b,c", after which get("a,b") never matches and returns None, while get("a") returns "b,c" -- a value it never wrote. Newlines in a key or value split one pair into two lines with the same class of effect. Deterministic and data-dependent: it either affects a given key on every read or never, which is why it is a ticket rather than a page, but the wrongness it produces is entirely silent.

payload_or_id.name: Every storage operation reads or rewrites the entire file
payload_or_id.description: get linear-scans the whole file to resolve one key and put reads and rewrites all of it to change one key, so both cost O(total keys) in time and I/O. Cost rises with the size of the store rather than with traffic, meaning the system degrades on a timescale governed by data growth and gives no warning tied to load. Compounded by the write path: as the file grows, put's rewrite window widens, which widens the exposure to the torn-read and truncation failures above.

payload_or_id.name: Data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The sole known writer is a job outside this repo. If it dies, is descheduled, wedges, or fails every attempt, storage simply stops changing. payload_or_id.name: Per-process caches diverge from each other

payload_or_id.name: Metrics never reach a scraper

Phase 2 accepted — 23 failure modes: 7 user-visible ends and 16 upstream links.

**The headline: 22 of 23 are invisible to current instrumentation.** Only `fm-storage-file-unreadable` → `fm-read-error-returned` is alertable today, and it's the *least* dangerous user-visible failure precisely because it's the loud one — the client knows the read failed instead of acting on a wrong answer. Every other user-visible failure returns HTTP-success-shaped data and increments `outcome="success"`.

**Four chains, each detectable well upstream of where a user notices:**

- **Staleness.** Two independent defects combine into permanence: the write path never calls `cache.evict`, and the eviction that would eventually retire the entry removes nothing. Either alone is survivable; together there is no path back to consistency short of a restart. A third route reaches the same symptom with no cache involvement at all — a stopped or failing writer leaves *storage* stale, so even a cold cache serves old data.
- **Unboundedness.** Same root defect as above (`fm-evictor-unit-mismatch`), different consequence: growth → OOM kill → restart → clean cache → repeat. That sawtooth reads as an infrastructure flap rather than a cache bug, which is why the upstream links matter more than the visible end.
- **Silent absence.** `Cache.get` tests `entry is not None` rather than membership, so a cached `None` is a hit. One read during any window where the file is missing or mid-rewrite pins that key to `None` for the process lifetime — the failure outlives its cause indefinitely.
- **Whole-store loss.** `put` truncates before writing, with no temp-and-rename, no lock, no fsync. The blast radius of one write is every key in the store, and the aftermath presents as ordinary successful responses.

**Two exclusions, both reasoned rather than dismissive:**
- `fm-evictor-unit-mismatch` — the root cause of two critical chains, but a broken predicate and a correct predicate with nothing to do emit the identical observation. Detection belongs one link downstream at `fm-eviction-removes-nothing`; an alert here would never fire or would duplicate that one. Fix by ticket.
- `fm-storage-comma-ambiguity` — a pure function of key content, so no onset, no rate, no threshold. Any rule would have to encode the correct answer, which *is* the fix. Its user-visible consequences stay covered where they're actually detectable.

One thing I want to flag as a judgement call for your review: I rated `fm-evictor-unit-mismatch` and `fm-eviction-removes-nothing` as **warning** despite them causing critical failures, on the grounds that severity should track what an operator can usefully do when woken. Growth gives hours-to-days of headroom; the staleness they enable is permanent but not resolvable at 3am either. If you'd rather severity track blast radius than actionability, those two and `fm-cache-unbounded-growth` should be critical, and phase 4's paging set roughly doubles.

event.text:
Phase 3 accepted: 1 implemented metric inventoried, 15 recommendations, all 23 failure modes' coverage set.

**Implemented instrumentation, in full:** `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`, declared at `api.py:19-23`, incremented at two call sites. That's the entire observability surface. Grep confirmed no other definition site, no `/metrics` endpoint, no `start_http_server`.

**Final coverage split:** 2 alertable, 19 metric-gap, 2 excluded.

The two alertable modes are the same chain (`fm-storage-file-unreadable` → `fm-read-error-returned`) — a rule today, no code change. I deliberately kept `fm-storage-file-unreadable` at *alertable* even though one recommendation would attribute it better; calling it a gap would misrepresent what the service can already see.

**Why the existing metric covers so little:** it counts call *outcomes*, not *answers*. A stale value, a poisoned `None`, and a correct value are one identical increment. Every silent-wrongness failure is invisible by construction, not by oversight.

**Sequencing that matters more than the list itself:**

1. **`mr-expose-metrics-registry` is a hard prerequisite.** Nothing serves the default registry. Until that's fixed, every metric here — existing and proposed — is written to memory and discarded, and no phase-4 alert can fire.
2. **`mr-eviction-entries-removed-total` is the highest-value single addition.** `run_eviction_pass` already computes the number and every caller throws it away. Recording it covers the root of *both* the unboundedness and staleness-recovery chains. Paired with a pass counter, it separates three states that are currently one observation: broken predicate, absent scheduler, genuinely idle cache.
3. **`mr-cache-invalidations-total` + `mr-write-operations-total`** solve what looked unsolvable. Detecting staleness directly would need the service to know the correct answer. But the invalidation gap shows up as a *structural contradiction* — writes climbing while `reason="writer"` invalidations stay at zero — which the service can observe about itself with certainty, before any user is served a stale value.

**Only one recommendation is a change rather than an addition:** splitting the existing counter's `success` into `success_found`/`success_absent`. I chose a label change over a parallel counter (which would double-count and need hand-maintained consistency), and it breaks continuity for anything matching `outcome="success"` — cheap here only because the sole such rule is one I'm about to propose.

**Two honest limits I want on the record rather than buried:**
- `fm-corrupt-value-served` is only *half* closed. Malformed-line counting catches the torn-read cause; the delimiter-collision cause has no detectable signal and needs the code fix. I marked it metric-gap rather than claiming the recommendation resolves it.
- `fm-cache-per-process-divergence` is detected as *disagreement between instances*, so it depends on per-instance exposition. A multiprocess collector that aggregates workers would erase exactly the variance that constitutes the evidence — worth deciding at exposition time, not after.

One sequencing hazard for phase 4: read latency is currently masked by a hit ratio near 1.0 that exists *only because eviction is broken*. Fixing eviction correctly restores miss traffic this system has never carried. The latency histograms should land before that fix, or the resulting change arrives unmeasured and gets misread as a regression caused by the fix.

Ready for phase 4 (alert recommendations).

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert
serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode
may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).

payload_or_id.name: process_resident_memory_bytes
payload_or_id.definition_site: prometheus_client library (PROCESS_COLLECTOR), auto-registered against the default registry on import -- reached in this codebase via `from prometheus_client import Counter` at kvstore/api.py:14
emission_sites: collected on scrape from /proc/self/statm; no call site in this codebase
payload_or_id.description: Implemented but not declared here, which is why the first pass of this inventory missed it: prometheus_client registers PROCESS_COLLECTOR, PLATFORM_COLLECTOR and GC_COLLECTOR against the default registry at import time, so importing it is enough to publish process_resident_memory_bytes, process_cpu_seconds_total, process_open_fds, process_start_time_seconds, python_gc_* and python_info. On Linux these are read from /proc and are real measurements, not stubs. Recorded because resident memory is the correct primary signal for fm-process-oom-outage: it measures the actual quantity that causes the kill, whereas kvstore_cache_entries is a proxy needing a bytes-per-entry assumption nobody has measured. It does not, however, attribute the growth -- resident memory rising says nothing about whether the cache or the workload is responsible, which is what mr-cache-entries-gauge supplies. The two are complementary rather than redundant. Caveat: like every metric here it is inert until mr-expose-metrics-registry is done, and under a multiprocess deployment the process collector describes only the process that served the scrape.

payload_or_id.rationale: Corrected from the first pass, which listed no implemented metric here. process_resident_memory_bytes comes free with prometheus_client's default registry and is the primary signal -- it measures the quantity that actually triggers the kill, and once exposition exists this failure is detectable with a rule over an already-implemented metric. Retained as metric-gap rather than promoted to alertable for two reasons: it is gated on mr-expose-metrics-registry, and resident memory alone cannot attribute growth to the cache, so it cannot distinguish this failure mode's chain from an unrelated memory regression. mr-cache-entries-gauge supplies that attribution and mr-eviction-entries-removed-total supplies the cause, which is what turns a page into a diagnosis.

Resident memory from the default collectors gives a coarse, already-implemented view of the growth once exposition exists, but it is genuinely insufficient here rather than merely less convenient: the failure mode is specifically that the cache dict grows without bound, and resident memory cannot separate that from a workload change, a memory leak elsewhere, or allocator behaviour. The entries gauge is the signal that makes the diagnosis, and the eviction counter explains why removal is not happening -- which determines whether the response is a restart or a code fix.

annotations.summary: More than 1% of kvstore reads are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: get_value is raising StorageError to clients. The underlying cause is an OSError reading the backing file: permission denial, an I/O error, a disappeared mount, or a descriptor limit. This is the only alert in this group that works against instrumentation already present in the codebase -- no code change is needed to deploy it, and it should be the first rule installed. Note what it does NOT cover, because the coverage is narrower than the name suggests: it detects loud failures only. A read that returns a stale, absent, or corrupt value is counted as a success and is invisible here. A silent kvstore is not a healthy one. clamp_min guards division by zero at low traffic; the ratio form avoids paging on a single error during a quiet period.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are running but have removed nothing for an hour
annotations.description: The pass is being invoked and completing, the cache has been continuously non-empty for the full hour, and TTL_SECONDS is 300 -- so entries older than the TTL certainly exist and something should have been removed. This is the signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds comparison in run_eviction_pass (fm-evictor-unit-mismatch), which phase 2 excluded from carrying its own alert precisely because this is where it becomes observable. Highest-leverage alert in the group: this one defect disables both cache boundedness and staleness recovery, so firing here pre-empts both the OOM chain and the permanent-stale-read chain. The three conjuncts matter: without the passes term this cannot distinguish a broken predicate from a dead scheduler, and without the cache-entries term it would fire on a legitimately empty cache.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has run for 30 minutes
annotations.description: run_eviction_pass is not being invoked. Nothing in the kvstore package schedules it -- the caller lives outside this repo -- so this covers the scheduler having died, being wedged, or never having been wired up at all. The absent() arm is not defensive padding: it is the case that matters most, because a scheduler that was never wired up produces no series whatsoever, and a rule written only as increase()==0 would evaluate against nothing and stay silent forever. Distinguish from KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing by which fires: this one means the pass is not running, that one means it runs and does nothing. Different fixes -- restart or wire up the scheduler here, correct the predicate there.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is rising steadily with no plateau
annotations.description: The cache has grown monotonically over six hours and, extrapolated, will exceed the configured entry budget within a day. Substitute 1000000 with the entry count this deployment has actually been tested to hold -- the placeholder is a starting point, not a measurement. Warning rather than critical because the timescale is hours to days, which is exactly the headroom this alert exists to buy: it should fire long before KvstoreMemoryExhaustionImminent. If it fires alongside KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing, the cause is the eviction defect rather than a workload change, and the fix is code rather than capacity.

annotations.summary: kvstore will exhaust its memory limit within about four hours
annotations.description: Resident memory is trending toward the container limit. Substitute 1073741824 (1 GiB) with this deployment's real limit. Uses process_resident_memory_bytes, which prometheus_client's default registry provides for free -- no new instrumentation needed beyond exposing the registry. Pages because the outcome is an OOM kill that drops every in-flight request, and because acting early converts it into a deliberate restart. Check KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded and KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing to attribute the growth: resident memory says the process is dying, not why. If restarts recur on a regular period, that sawtooth is the unbounded cache, not an infrastructure flap -- treat a repeating pattern here as a code defect rather than as capacity.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache entry has been invalidated by the writer
annotations.description: Storage has been written and the cache has not been told, so any key already cached now serves a value the store no longer holds -- and with eviction inert there is no path back to consistency short of a restart. Detects a structural contradiction rather than staleness itself, which is the point: recognising a stale value would require the service to know the correct answer, whereas 'writes happened, invalidations did not' is a fact it can observe with certainty. Fires before any user is served a wrong value. Written with `unless` over aggregated series deliberately: kvstore_cache_invalidations_total{reason="writer"} will not exist at all while the defect is present, since prometheus_client only creates a child series once .labels() is called, and a naive `and increase(...) == 0` would evaluate against an empty vector and never fire. The fix is one line -- call cache.evict(key) in admin.update_value.

annotations.summary: No write has succeeded in over two hours
annotations.description: The data-sync job has stopped writing, or every attempt is failing. Storage itself is now stale, so even a cold cache serves old data -- this reaches users without any cache involvement at all. Substitute 7200 with twice the real sync interval. Expressed as wall-clock age rather than a counter rate on purpose: for an hourly or daily cadence, a rate of zero over any short window is indistinguishable from a normal gap between runs, so a rate-based rule would either miss a stopped writer for hours or fire constantly. This is the earliest link in the whole-store staleness chain and the one with the most headroom before users notice. Check KvstoreWriteErrors to tell a failing writer from an absent one.

annotations.summary: A write to the backing store has failed
annotations.description: Storage.put raised StorageError -- a full disk, a read-only or remounted filesystem, permission denial, or a quota breach. Threshold is any occurrence rather than a rate: writes are low-volume and every one that fails is data that did not land, so there is no benign background level to tolerate. Readers see no error from this at all; they see data that quietly stopped changing, which is why this needs its own alert rather than being inferred from the read path. Note the compounding risk: put truncates the file before rewriting it, so a write failing partway through can leave the store truncated -- check KvstoreStoreEmptied and KvstoreStoreShrankSharply when this fires.

annotations.summary: The backing file does not exist -- every key is reading as absent
annotations.description: Storage.get found no file at its configured path and returned None without raising, so the service is silently reporting an empty store: deletion, a wrong or unmounted path, an empty volume after a redeploy, or a fresh host that never received the data. Urgent beyond the immediate outage because of what it leaves behind -- every read during this window is cached as a negative entry, and with eviction inert those keys keep returning None long after the file is restored. Restoring the file is therefore necessary but not sufficient; the process must also be restarted to clear the poisoned entries. Short for_duration because the poisoning accrues continuously while this is true.

annotations.summary: The store holds zero keys but held data within the last 24 hours
annotations.description: Total data loss. Storage.put truncates the file before writing it, with no temp-file-and-rename and no fsync, so a crash, kill, container eviction, or disk-full condition mid-write destroys every key not re-written -- the blast radius of a single write is the entire store. The most severe failure in this analysis and entirely silent without this metric: reads afterwards return None with no error and are counted as successes. The 24h lookback distinguishes real loss from a legitimately fresh, empty deployment. Restore from backup and restart the process: negative entries cached during the outage survive the restore.

annotations.summary: The store lost more than half its keys within an hour
annotations.description: Catches partial truncation, which KvstoreStoreEmptied misses because the file is left non-empty. Causes: an interrupted whole-file rewrite, or a lost update where one writer's full-file rewrite discarded everything another had written. A key count should only ever fall through deliberate deletion, and this service has no delete operation at all -- so any material drop is data loss by definition, not normal operation. Carries critical severity as the highest among the failure modes it serves. Pair with KvstoreStorageParseAnomalies, which fires when the truncation is caught while being read rather than after the fact.

annotations.summary: Malformed lines found in the backing store -- a torn or truncated write
annotations.description: A line with no comma cannot be produced by a completed put, so encountering one is direct evidence the file was read mid-rewrite or left truncated by an interrupted one. Today this is entirely silent: partition() on a malformed line returns empty strings and the loop continues without complaint, so the only symptom is a wrong value reaching a user. Urgent because the damage persists: a value read during the torn window is cached and returned identically until restart, so a race lasting milliseconds becomes a wrong answer lasting indefinitely. Critical as the highest severity among the modes served. The alert is a detector, not a remedy -- the fix is writing to a temp file and renaming.

annotations.summary: Over 5% of cache lookups are returning a cached absent value
annotations.description: Keys are pinned to None. Cache.get tests `entry is not None` rather than testing membership, so a cached None counts as a hit and never reads through to storage again -- one read taken while the file was missing, mid-rewrite, or simply not yet written poisons that key for the entire process lifetime. The user-visible failure therefore long outlives whatever caused it, and no error is raised at any point. Tune the 5% threshold to the workload: a service legitimately queried for unknown keys will carry a baseline, and what matters is a rise above it. Remediation is a restart to clear the poisoned entries plus fixing the membership test; restoring the data alone will not help.

annotations.summary: Over a quarter of reads are returning no value
annotations.description: The user-boundary view of silent data loss: clients are being told keys have no value. Requires the label change splitting outcome="success" into success_found and success_absent -- today both are one increment, which is why this whole failure class is invisible at the exact place users experience it. Deliberately the least specific alert in the group and the last to be believed on its own: it fires for a missing file, a truncated store, poisoned negative cache entries, or simply a change in what clients ask for. Use it to confirm user impact and reach for KvstoreBackingFileMissing, KvstoreStoreEmptied, and KvstoreNegativeCacheHitsElevated to attribute the cause. Threshold assumes a workload dominated by hits; set it from the observed baseline.

annotations.summary: Two or more writes were in flight at once -- lost updates are possible
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the whole file, so overlapping writers each rewrite everything and the later one wins wholesale, silently discarding the other's keys. Alerts on the precondition rather than the loss because the loss leaves no trace: both writers returned successfully and nothing records that the discarded key was ever written. Phase 2 could only record this failure as conditional on an unverified deployment assumption -- whether more than one writer exists -- and this alert settles that question with evidence. Warning rather than critical: it reports that the window is being entered, not that data was definitely lost. If it ever fires, treat the single-writer assumption as refuted and add locking or serialise the writers.

annotations.summary: p99 read latency above 500ms
annotations.description: Users are waiting on reads, and any client-side timeout turns this into an error for them. The cause is a cache miss falling through to a linear scan of the entire backing file, so latency scales with the number of stored keys rather than with traffic -- it degrades on a data-growth timescale and gives no load-correlated warning. Expect this to appear when the eviction defect is fixed: the current near-1.0 hit ratio exists only because nothing is ever evicted, so restoring correct expiry restores miss traffic this system has never carried. That is the fix working as intended, not a regression it caused -- but it means this histogram must be deployed before that fix, or the change arrives unmeasured. Substitute a threshold from the real client timeout.

annotations.summary: p99 storage operation latency above 250ms
annotations.description: Attributes slowness to the store itself, split by operation so a slow whole-file scan (get) is distinguishable from a slow whole-file rewrite (put). Both are O(total keys) and both will keep worsening as the store grows, since neither has an index. The put series carries a second meaning worth acting on independently: it measures how long the file spends truncated or partially written, which is the exposure window for torn reads and for total loss on an interrupted write. A rising put duration means KvstoreStorageParseAnomalies and KvstoreStoreEmptied are becoming more likely over time -- a leading indicator of two critical failures, not merely a performance concern.

annotations.summary: Worker caches differ by more than half their size
annotations.description: The cache is a plain in-process dict with no sharing, so each worker holds an independent view populated at different times. Large divergence means the same key can return different values depending on which process serves the request -- which is what makes every staleness failure present intermittently and non-reproducibly, the property that makes such user reports hardest to diagnose. Two caveats, both material. Some divergence is normal after a rolling restart, hence the 30m for_duration and a deliberately loose threshold. More importantly this alert only works if each instance is scraped separately: a multiprocess collector that aggregates workers erases exactly the variance that constitutes the evidence, so the exposition choice made for KvstoreMetricsMissing determines whether this rule can ever fire.

While the defect is present, `kvstore_cache_invalidations_total{reason="writer"}` **does not exist** — prometheus_client only creates a child series once `.labels()` is called. The naive form evaluates against an empty vector and stays silent exactly when the bug is live.

payload_or_id.description: StorageError propagates out of get_value to the client. The only user-visible failure this service can already measure: the counter increments under outcome="error" before the re-raise, so no new instrumentation is required and a rule alone suffices. Corrected in this amendment: the original text claimed it was 'alertable today with a rule alone and no code change', which was wrong. It is also the least dangerous of the user-visible failures precisely because it is loud -- the client knows the read failed, rather than acting on a wrong answer. It does not poison the cache: the exception propagates before any entry is inserted, so recovery is immediate once the underlying condition clears.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file read raises OSError
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get wraps its read in try/except OSError and raises StorageError. Covers permission denial, an I/O error, a disappeared mount, and a descriptor or memory limit hit while reading the whole file. Unlike the absent-file case this one is loud: it propagates through get_value, which increments kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} before re-raising. Corrected in this amendment: the original text called this 'the one failure in this document already covered by existing instrumentation -- alertable with a rule alone and no code change'. payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache._entries only ever gains keys. Insertion happens on every miss, including misses that resolve to None, and the sole removal path is Cache.evict, which is called only by an eviction pass that removes nothing. Under sustained unique-key traffic the dict grows monotonically for the lifetime of the process, bounded only by available memory. Warning rather than critical because it degrades over hours or days rather than instantly, leaving time to act. Corrected in this amendment: the original text ended 'but only if something is watching, and no entry count is exported today', which overstated the blindness. No entry count is exported -- that part stands -- but process_resident_memory_bytes comes free with prometheus_client's default collectors, so once exposition exists the growth is coarsely observable as rising memory. That is genuinely insufficient here rather than merely less convenient: the claim this failure mode makes is specifically that the cache dict grows without bound, and resident memory cannot separate that from a workload change, a leak elsewhere, or allocator behaviour. Hence still metric-gap, and mr-cache-entries-gauge is what supplies the attribution that turns an observation into a diagnosis.

payload_or_id.title: Process is killed for exhausting memory
payload_or_id.description: The unbounded cache eventually exhausts the process or container memory limit and the process is OOM-killed, taking every in-flight request with it. Total loss of service until restart, and restart clears the cache, so the system recovers fully and then walks the same path again on a period set by traffic -- a sawtooth that reads as an infrastructure flap rather than as a cache defect. The final link of the boundedness chain and the only one users perceive; every link above it is detectable hours or days earlier. Amended: this failure mode is better served by implemented instrumentation than the original text implied. process_resident_memory_bytes, auto-registered by prometheus_client, measures the exact quantity that causes the kill, and is a more direct signal than the recommended cache-entry gauge, which is a proxy requiring a bytes-per-entry ratio nobody has measured. Retained as metric-gap on two grounds: it is gated on exposition, and resident memory alone cannot attribute the growth to the cache, so it cannot distinguish this chain from an unrelated memory regression -- which is the difference between paging someone and telling them what to fix.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics never reach a scraper
payload_or_id.description: Nothing in this repo exposes the default registry: no start_http_server, no ASGI or WSGI metrics app, no push gateway. Whatever exposes it lives outside this repo, unverified. If that path is absent, misconfigured, or the scrape target is wrong or down, everything the registry holds is written to memory and discarded. Amended: the original text framed the loss as 'every counter increment', scoped to the single Counter this codebase declares. The registry holds more than that -- prometheus_client auto-registers process, platform and GC collectors on import, so this failure also discards process_resident_memory_bytes and its siblings, which the amendment established as the primary available signal for the OOM chain. The blast radius is therefore wider than recorded: it blocks not only the instrumentation that has to be written but the instrumentation that already exists for free. Critical, and first to confirm, because it is the common single point of failure beneath every alert in phases 3 and 4: a broken scrape path presents as a silent, permanently healthy-looking service, which is the same picture as a service with no traffic. Detecting it cannot rely on the service's own metrics and needs an external liveness signal.

payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_eviction_passes_total, incremented once per completed pass at the end of run_eviction_pass in kvstore/evictor.py. No labels. Must be paired with mr-eviction-entries-removed-total; neither is diagnostic alone. A flat counter here means the scheduler is not calling in, and is the earliest signal in the boundedness chain, hours to days ahead of fm-process-oom-outage.

payload_or_id.rationale: The highest-value single addition in this document: one counter covering the root of both the unboundedness chain and the staleness-recovery chain. The value is already computed and returned by run_eviction_pass and discarded by every caller, so this records an existing number rather than deriving a new one. It is also the designated detection point for fm-evictor-unit-mismatch, which phase 2 excluded from carrying its own alert precisely because it surfaces here -- that mode is deliberately absent from the linkage above, since its coverage row carries no recommendation and an excluded mode needs no mapping.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_eviction_entries_removed_total, incremented by len(expired_keys) in run_eviction_pass in kvstore/evictor.py. No labels. Read together with mr-eviction-passes-total the defect signature is unmistakable and available immediately: passes climbing while removals stay pinned at zero. That pair distinguishes a broken predicate from an absent scheduler from a genuinely idle cache, three states that are currently one observation.

payload_or_id.rationale: The direct headroom signal for the unboundedness chain and the one an operator can actually act on: a monotonic rise with no plateau predicts the OOM kill with enough lead time to restart deliberately rather than be paged by the crash.
payload_or_id.details: New gauge kvstore_cache_entries, set to len(self._entries) after insertion in Cache.get and after removal in Cache.evict, in kvstore/cache.py. Preferable to inferring size from eviction counters because it survives restarts honestly -- it drops to zero, which is exactly the sawtooth that identifies fm-process-oom-outage as a cache defect rather than the infrastructure flap it currently resembles. Across instances, divergence in this gauge is the most direct evidence of fm-cache-per-process-divergence. Emit no per-key label under any circumstance: key cardinality is unbounded by definition here.

payload_or_id.rationale: The negative_hit label value is the only way to see fm-negative-result-cached, where a key poisoned by one badly-timed read is served None forever while the entrypoint counts every one of those reads as a success. A rising negative_hit rate is the earliest and most specific evidence of fm-missing-value-served.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_cache_lookups_total, labelled `result`, incremented on each of the three paths through Cache.get in kvstore/cache.py. Three label values: "hit" (entry present with a value), "negative_hit" (entry present holding None), "miss" (read through to storage). The hit/miss split additionally makes the eviction defect visible from a second, independent direction -- a hit ratio that only climbs toward 1.0 and never decays is what a cache that never expires anything looks like -- corroborating mr-eviction-entries-removed-total from the read path rather than the worker. No key label.

payload_or_id.rationale: Detecting staleness directly would require the service to know the correct answer, which it cannot. The invalidation gap is instead visible as a structural contradiction the service can observe about itself with certainty: writes occurring while invalidations with reason="writer" remain at zero. That catches fm-writer-skips-cache-invalidation before any user is served a stale value, with no oracle needed.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_cache_invalidations_total, labelled `reason`, incremented in Cache.evict in kvstore/cache.py with the reason supplied by the caller. Label values "writer" and "ttl". Keeps working after the eviction defect is fixed, when reason="ttl" starts moving and the writer path's continued silence would otherwise be masked by non-zero total invalidations. Pairs with mr-write-operations-total, which supplies the other half of the contradiction.

payload_or_id.rationale: The write path is entirely uninstrumented, which is why fm-storage-write-fails is invisible: StorageError propagates to a job outside this repo and outside the read counter's reach, so a write path failing every attempt produces no signal anywhere while readers see only data that quietly stopped changing.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_write_operations_total, labelled `outcome` with values "success" and "error", wrapped around the storage.put call in update_value in kvstore/admin.py. Closes the hole at the point the exception is already visible, requiring no new error handling. Also the denominator for the invalidation-gap detector -- 'writes happening, invalidations not' needs both halves.

payload_or_id.rationale: A counter's rate cannot express 'this should have happened by now' for a job whose cadence may be hourly or daily: zero over a five-minute window is indistinguishable from a normal gap between runs, so any rate-based rule either misses a stopped writer for a long time or fires constantly. Wall-clock age since last success states the condition directly and thresholds cleanly against the known sync interval.
payload_or_id.details: New gauge kvstore_last_successful_write_timestamp_seconds, set to the current unix time after storage.put returns successfully in kvstore/admin.py. No labels. Complements rather than duplicates mr-write-operations-total. This is the earliest link in the whole-store staleness chain and the one with the most headroom before users are affected, which is exactly what makes it worth a dedicated metric rather than an inference.

payload_or_id.rationale: The `file_missing` outcome is the critical distinction. Storage.get treats a vanished backing file as an empty store and returns None with no error, so deletion, a wrong path, an unmounted volume, and an empty volume after a redeploy are currently indistinguishable from a legitimately unknown key. Splitting it out turns fm-storage-file-absent from undetectable into one unambiguous series.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_storage_operations_total in kvstore/storage.py, labelled `operation` in {get, put} and `outcome` in {found, absent, file_missing, error}. Bounded cardinality: two operations, four outcomes. Also gives fm-whole-store-loss a signal at the storage layer rather than only at its user-visible end. Not linked to fm-storage-file-unreadable, which its coverage row classes alertable on already-implemented instrumentation: this would improve attribution there but is not required for detection, and linking it would misreport that mode as depending on new work.

payload_or_id.rationale: Today a returned None and a returned value are the same increment, so the entire class of silent-absence failures is invisible at the exact boundary the user experiences. Splitting the success label makes it countable there, which is where a user-visible failure should be measured even though upstream metrics attribute it better.
payload_or_id.details: The one change to an existing metric rather than an addition. Replace "success" with "success_found" and "success_absent" on kvstore_get_value_requests_total, keeping "error" as is; the declaration at kvstore/api.py:19-23 is unchanged and the call site at kvstore/api.py:32 splits on whether value is None. Deliberately a label change rather than a new parallel counter: a second counter alongside this one would double-count every request and leave two series to be kept consistent by hand. The cost is a continuity break for anything matching outcome="success" -- worth naming explicitly, and cheap here because the only such rule is one this analysis is proposing anyway. Cardinality rises from 2 series to 3. Never add a key label.

payload_or_id.rationale: Serves two failures on very different timescales from one series. Abruptly, a collapse to zero or a steep drop is the signature of fm-whole-store-loss, where the truncate-then-write in put destroys every key not re-written and nothing observes it. Gradually, the same gauge leads fm-read-latency-degradation and fm-storage-whole-file-io, which scale with exactly this number and degrade on a data-growth timescale that produces no load-correlated warning.
payload_or_id.details: New gauge kvstore_storage_keys in kvstore/storage.py, set to len(existing) after a successful put and to the parsed line count after a successful full read in get. No labels. Caveat worth recording: if set only on put, the gauge goes stale precisely when the writer stops -- the moment its value matters most -- so it should also be refreshed on the whole-file read that get already performs, which costs nothing extra.

payload_or_id.rationale: A line with no comma cannot be produced by a completed put, so encountering one is direct evidence the file was read mid-rewrite or left truncated by an interrupted one. Both are silent today because partition() on a malformed line returns empty strings and the loop continues without complaint.
payload_or_id.details: New counter kvstore_storage_parse_anomalies_total, no labels, incremented in the line loops of Storage.get and Storage.put in kvstore/storage.py wherever partition finds no comma. Converts a race that currently manifests only as a wrong answer served to a user into a countable event at the layer where it happens. A detector, not a fix: the fix is write-to-temp-then-rename, and this metric is what tells you whether the race actually occurs in production and whether the fix worked.

payload_or_id.rationale: Detects the precondition rather than the loss, because the loss is unobservable after the fact: both writers returned successfully and the file simply lacks one of their keys, with no record it ever held it. Overlapping puts, by contrast, are directly observable -- this gauge exceeding 1 proves the unsynchronised read-modify-write window is being entered concurrently.
payload_or_id.details: New gauge kvstore_storage_put_in_flight, no labels, incremented on entry to Storage.put and decremented on exit in kvstore/storage.py. Phase 2 recorded fm-concurrent-write-lost-update as conditional on a deployment fact this analysis could not verify -- whether more than one writer exists. This metric settles that question with evidence instead of assumption, which is why it is worth adding even though the failure may be unreachable in the current deployment.

payload_or_id.rationale: No metric anywhere in this service measures duration, so the user-visible half of fm-read-latency-degradation -- what the client actually waits for -- is unmeasured. Timing matters here: read latency is currently masked by a hit ratio near 1.0 sustained by the broken eviction, so fixing eviction correctly will restore miss traffic this system has never seen. This histogram should be in place before that fix ships, or the resulting latency change arrives unmeasured.
payload_or_id.details: New histogram kvstore_get_value_duration_seconds, no labels, wrapping the cache.get call in get_value in kvstore/api.py. Pairs with mr-storage-operation-duration-seconds rather than replacing it: this one states whether users are affected, that one attributes the cause.

payload_or_id.rationale: Attributes latency to the whole-file scan and whole-file rewrite, distinguishing a slow read caused by store growth from one caused by the filesystem itself, and making the O(total keys) cost measurable rather than merely inferable from mr-storage-keys-gauge.
payload_or_id.details: New histogram kvstore_storage_operation_duration_seconds, labelled `operation`, around the bodies of Storage.get and Storage.put in kvstore/storage.py. The put series has a second use, which is why fm-storage-nonatomic-rewrite is linked here as well: it measures the width of the window during which the file is truncated or partially written, so a rewrite duration trending upward means that race is getting likelier over time.

annotations.summary: kvstore is not being scraped -- every other kvstore alert is blind
annotations.description: Either no kvstore target exists in this Prometheus at all (absent) or every target is failing to scrape (up == 0). This is the meta-alert: kvstore's own instrumentation cannot detect this condition, because a process whose metrics never arrive is indistinguishable from a healthy, idle one, and every other rule in this group silently stops being able to fire. Check that the process exposes the registry (there is no start_http_server or metrics app in the kvstore package itself -- exposition is wired outside it), that the scrape target and port are correct, and that the process is running. Treat a firing of this alert as invalidating the silence of all other kvstore alerts for the same period, not as an isolated infrastructure issue.

annotations.summary: More than 1% of kvstore reads are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: get_value is raising StorageError to clients. The underlying cause is an OSError reading the backing file: permission denial, an I/O error, a disappeared mount, or a descriptor limit. This is the only rule in this group that needs no new measurement -- the counter it reads is already in the code -- but it is not deployable today: nothing in this repo exposes the default registry, so it cannot fire until the exposition gap (fm-metrics-not-exposed) is closed. Note what it does NOT cover, because the coverage is narrower than the name suggests: it detects loud failures only. A read that returns a stale, absent, or corrupt value is counted as a success and is invisible here. A silent kvstore is not a healthy one. clamp_min guards division by zero at low traffic; the ratio form avoids paging on a single error during a quiet period.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are running but have removed nothing for an hour
annotations.description: The pass is being invoked and completing, the cache has been continuously non-empty for the full hour, and TTL_SECONDS is 300 -- so entries older than the TTL certainly exist and something should have been removed. This is the signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds comparison in run_eviction_pass (fm-evictor-unit-mismatch), which phase 2 excluded from carrying its own alert precisely because this is where it becomes observable. Highest-leverage alert in the group: this one defect disables both cache boundedness and staleness recovery, so firing here pre-empts both the OOM chain and the permanent-stale-read chain. The three conjuncts matter: without the passes term this cannot distinguish a broken predicate from a dead scheduler, and without the cache-entries term it would fire on a legitimately empty cache.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has run for 30 minutes
annotations.description: run_eviction_pass is not being invoked. Nothing in the kvstore package schedules it -- the caller lives outside this repo -- so this covers the scheduler having died, being wedged, or never having been wired up at all. The absent() arm is not defensive padding: it is the case that matters most, because a scheduler that was never wired up produces no series whatsoever, and a rule written only as increase()==0 would evaluate against nothing and stay silent forever. Distinguish from KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing by which fires: this one means the pass is not running, that one means it runs and does nothing. Different fixes -- restart or wire up the scheduler here, correct the predicate there.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is rising steadily with no plateau
annotations.description: The cache has grown monotonically over six hours and, extrapolated, will exceed the configured entry budget within a day. Substitute 1000000 with the entry count this deployment has actually been tested to hold -- the placeholder is a starting point, not a measurement. Warning rather than critical because the timescale is hours to days, which is exactly the headroom this alert exists to buy: it should fire long before KvstoreMemoryExhaustionImminent. If it fires alongside KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing, the cause is the eviction defect rather than a workload change, and the fix is code rather than capacity.

annotations.summary: kvstore will exhaust its memory limit within about four hours
annotations.description: Resident memory is trending toward the container limit. Substitute 1073741824 (1 GiB) with this deployment's real limit. Uses process_resident_memory_bytes, which prometheus_client's default registry provides for free -- no new instrumentation needed beyond exposing the registry. Pages because the outcome is an OOM kill that drops every in-flight request, and because acting early converts it into a deliberate restart. Check KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded and KvstoreEvictionRemovesNothing to attribute the growth: resident memory says the process is dying, not why. If restarts recur on a regular period, that sawtooth is the unbounded cache, not an infrastructure flap -- treat a repeating pattern here as a code defect rather than as capacity.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache entry has been invalidated by the writer
annotations.description: Storage has been written and the cache has not been told, so any key already cached now serves a value the store no longer holds -- and with eviction inert there is no path back to consistency short of a restart. Detects a structural contradiction rather than staleness itself, which is the point: recognising a stale value would require the service to know the correct answer, whereas 'writes happened, invalidations did not' is a fact it can observe with certainty. Fires before any user is served a wrong value. Written with `unless` over aggregated series deliberately: kvstore_cache_invalidations_total{reason="writer"} will not exist at all while the defect is present, since prometheus_client only creates a child series once .labels() is called, and a naive `and increase(...) == 0` would evaluate against an empty vector and never fire. The fix is one line -- call cache.evict(key) in admin.update_value.

annotations.summary: No write has succeeded in over two hours
annotations.description: The data-sync job has stopped writing, or every attempt is failing. Storage itself is now stale, so even a cold cache serves old data -- this reaches users without any cache involvement at all. Substitute 7200 with twice the real sync interval. Expressed as wall-clock age rather than a counter rate on purpose: for an hourly or daily cadence, a rate of zero over any short window is indistinguishable from a normal gap between runs, so a rate-based rule would either miss a stopped writer for hours or fire constantly. This is the earliest link in the whole-store staleness chain and the one with the most headroom before users notice. Check KvstoreWriteErrors to tell a failing writer from an absent one.

annotations.summary: A write to the backing store has failed
annotations.description: Storage.put raised StorageError -- a full disk, a read-only or remounted filesystem, permission denial, or a quota breach. Threshold is any occurrence rather than a rate: writes are low-volume and every one that fails is data that did not land, so there is no benign background level to tolerate. Readers see no error from this at all; they see data that quietly stopped changing, which is why this needs its own alert rather than being inferred from the read path. Note the compounding risk: put truncates the file before rewriting it, so a write failing partway through can leave the store truncated -- check KvstoreStoreEmptied and KvstoreStoreShrankSharply when this fires.

annotations.summary: The backing file does not exist -- every key is reading as absent
annotations.description: Storage.get found no file at its configured path and returned None without raising, so the service is silently reporting an empty store: deletion, a wrong or unmounted path, an empty volume after a redeploy, or a fresh host that never received the data. Urgent beyond the immediate outage because of what it leaves behind -- every read during this window is cached as a negative entry, and with eviction inert those keys keep returning None long after the file is restored. Restoring the file is therefore necessary but not sufficient; the process must also be restarted to clear the poisoned entries. Short for_duration because the poisoning accrues continuously while this is true.

annotations.summary: The store holds zero keys but held data within the last 24 hours
annotations.description: Total data loss. Storage.put truncates the file before writing it, with no temp-file-and-rename and no fsync, so a crash, kill, container eviction, or disk-full condition mid-write destroys every key not re-written -- the blast radius of a single write is the entire store. The most severe failure in this analysis and entirely silent without this metric: reads afterwards return None with no error and are counted as successes. The 24h lookback distinguishes real loss from a legitimately fresh, empty deployment. Restore from backup and restart the process: negative entries cached during the outage survive the restore.

annotations.summary: The store lost more than half its keys within an hour
annotations.description: Catches partial truncation, which KvstoreStoreEmptied misses because the file is left non-empty. Causes: an interrupted whole-file rewrite, or a lost update where one writer's full-file rewrite discarded everything another had written. A key count should only ever fall through deliberate deletion, and this service has no delete operation at all -- so any material drop is data loss by definition, not normal operation. Carries critical severity as the highest among the failure modes it serves. Pair with KvstoreStorageParseAnomalies, which fires when the truncation is caught while being read rather than after the fact.

annotations.summary: Malformed lines found in the backing store -- a torn or truncated write
annotations.description: A line with no comma cannot be produced by a completed put, so encountering one is direct evidence the file was read mid-rewrite or left truncated by an interrupted one. Today this is entirely silent: partition() on a malformed line returns empty strings and the loop continues without complaint, so the only symptom is a wrong value reaching a user. Urgent because the damage persists: a value read during the torn window is cached and returned identically until restart, so a race lasting milliseconds becomes a wrong answer lasting indefinitely. Critical as the highest severity among the modes served. The alert is a detector, not a remedy -- the fix is writing to a temp file and renaming.

annotations.summary: Over 5% of cache lookups are returning a cached absent value
annotations.description: Keys are pinned to None. Cache.get tests `entry is not None` rather than testing membership, so a cached None counts as a hit and never reads through to storage again -- one read taken while the file was missing, mid-rewrite, or simply not yet written poisons that key for the entire process lifetime. The user-visible failure therefore long outlives whatever caused it, and no error is raised at any point. Tune the 5% threshold to the workload: a service legitimately queried for unknown keys will carry a baseline, and what matters is a rise above it. Remediation is a restart to clear the poisoned entries plus fixing the membership test; restoring the data alone will not help.

annotations.summary: Over a quarter of reads are returning no value
annotations.description: The user-boundary view of silent data loss: clients are being told keys have no value. Requires the label change splitting outcome="success" into success_found and success_absent -- today both are one increment, which is why this whole failure class is invisible at the exact place users experience it. Deliberately the least specific alert in the group and the last to be believed on its own: it fires for a missing file, a truncated store, poisoned negative cache entries, or simply a change in what clients ask for. Use it to confirm user impact and reach for KvstoreBackingFileMissing, KvstoreStoreEmptied, and KvstoreNegativeCacheHitsElevated to attribute the cause. Threshold assumes a workload dominated by hits; set it from the observed baseline.

annotations.summary: Two or more writes were in flight at once -- lost updates are possible
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the whole file, so overlapping writers each rewrite everything and the later one wins wholesale, silently discarding the other's keys. Alerts on the precondition rather than the loss because the loss leaves no trace: both writers returned successfully and nothing records that the discarded key was ever written. Phase 2 could only record this failure as conditional on an unverified deployment assumption -- whether more than one writer exists -- and this alert settles that question with evidence. Warning rather than critical: it reports that the window is being entered, not that data was definitely lost. If it ever fires, treat the single-writer assumption as refuted and add locking or serialise the writers.

annotations.summary: p99 read latency above 500ms
annotations.description: Users are waiting on reads, and any client-side timeout turns this into an error for them. The cause is a cache miss falling through to a linear scan of the entire backing file, so latency scales with the number of stored keys rather than with traffic -- it degrades on a data-growth timescale and gives no load-correlated warning. Expect this to appear when the eviction defect is fixed: the current near-1.0 hit ratio exists only because nothing is ever evicted, so restoring correct expiry restores miss traffic this system has never carried. That is the fix working as intended, not a regression it caused -- but it means this histogram must be deployed before that fix, or the change arrives unmeasured. Substitute a threshold from the real client timeout.

annotations.summary: p99 storage operation latency above 250ms
annotations.description: Attributes slowness to the store itself, split by operation so a slow whole-file scan (get) is distinguishable from a slow whole-file rewrite (put). Both are O(total keys) and both will keep worsening as the store grows, since neither has an index. The put series carries a second meaning worth acting on independently: it measures how long the file spends truncated or partially written, which is the exposure window for torn reads and for total loss on an interrupted write. A rising put duration means KvstoreStorageParseAnomalies and KvstoreStoreEmptied are becoming more likely over time -- a leading indicator of two critical failures, not merely a performance concern.

annotations.summary: Worker caches differ by more than half their size
annotations.description: The cache is a plain in-process dict with no sharing, so each worker holds an independent view populated at different times. Large divergence means the same key can return different values depending on which process serves the request -- which is what makes every staleness failure present intermittently and non-reproducibly, the property that makes such user reports hardest to diagnose. Two caveats, both material. Some divergence is normal after a rolling restart, hence the 30m for_duration and a deliberately loose threshold. More importantly this alert only works if each instance is scraped separately: a multiprocess collector that aggregates workers erases exactly the variance that constitutes the evidence, so the exposition choice made for KvstoreMetricsMissing determines whether this rule can ever fire.
