payload_or_id.name: kvstore_get_value_requests_total
payload_or_id.description: The only metric this codebase declares. A Counter defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23 at module import, against prometheus_client's default registry, with a single label `outcome` taking exactly two values: "error", incremented at kvstore/api.py:30 when StorageError propagates out of cache.get and before it is re-raised, and "success", incremented at kvstore/api.py:32 on every other return. What it can see: the rate and proportion of reads that raised StorageError, which makes fm-storage-file-unreadable and its user-visible end fm-read-error-returned detectable with a rule alone. What it cannot see, and this is the substance of the coverage picture: it counts call outcomes, not answers. A cache hit returning a superseded value, a cached None for a populated key, and a correct value are all one increment of outcome="success", so every silent-wrongness failure mode is invisible here by construction. It is also read-path only -- no write, cache, eviction, or storage operation is counted anywhere -- and carries no notion of whether the value returned was found or absent. Exposition is unverified: nothing in this repo serves the default registry, so whether these increments ever leave the process is a deployment fact outside the codebase (fm-metrics-not-exposed).

payload_or_id.name: process_resident_memory_bytes
payload_or_id.description: Implemented but not declared in this codebase, which is why the first pass of this inventory missed it. prometheus_client registers PROCESS_COLLECTOR, PLATFORM_COLLECTOR and GC_COLLECTOR against the default registry at import time, so the `from prometheus_client import Counter` at kvstore/api.py:14 -- cited above as the emission site because it is the only line in this repo that causes the metric to exist -- is enough to publish process_resident_memory_bytes, process_cpu_seconds_total, process_open_fds, process_start_time_seconds, python_gc_* and python_info. There is no per-observation call site: the value is read from /proc/self/statm when a scrape arrives. On Linux these are real measurements, not stubs. Recorded because resident memory is the correct primary signal for fm-process-oom-outage: it measures the actual quantity that causes the kill, whereas kvstore_cache_entries is a proxy needing a bytes-per-entry assumption nobody has measured. It does not attribute the growth -- resident memory rising says nothing about whether the cache or the workload is responsible, which is what mr-cache-entries-gauge supplies. Caveat: inert until mr-expose-metrics-registry is done, and under a multiprocess deployment the process collector describes only the process that served the scrape.

payload_or_id.description: StorageError propagates out of get_value to the client. The only user-visible failure this service can already measure: kvstore_get_value_requests_total increments under outcome="error" before the re-raise, so no new instrumentation is needed and only a rule is missing -- which is what classes it alertable. That classification is about measurement, not deployability: nothing in this repo exposes the default registry, so no rule can actually fire until fm-metrics-not-exposed is resolved. The exposition gate is carried once, as its own critical entry, rather than repeated as a qualifier on every row, which would collapse the alertable/metric-gap distinction to nothing. This is also the least dangerous of the user-visible failures precisely because it is loud -- the client knows the read failed, rather than acting on a wrong answer. It does not poison the cache: the exception propagates before any entry is inserted, so recovery is immediate once the underlying condition clears.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file read raises OSError
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get wraps its read in try/except OSError and raises StorageError. Covers permission denial, an I/O error, a disappeared mount, and a descriptor or memory limit hit while reading the whole file. Unlike the absent-file case this one is loud: it propagates through get_value, which increments kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} before re-raising. It is the only failure mode here whose detection needs nothing but a rule -- though, like every rule in this analysis, it cannot fire until the registry is exposed (fm-metrics-not-exposed). It is not the only mode touched by already-implemented metrics: prometheus_client's default collectors publish process_resident_memory_bytes, which bears on fm-process-oom-outage.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache._entries only ever gains keys. Insertion happens on every miss, including misses that resolve to None, and the sole removal path is Cache.evict, which is called only by an eviction pass that removes nothing. Under sustained unique-key traffic the dict grows monotonically for the lifetime of the process, bounded only by available memory. Warning rather than critical because it degrades over hours or days rather than instantly, leaving time to act. Partially observable already: process_resident_memory_bytes comes free with prometheus_client's default collectors, so once exposition exists the growth shows up as rising memory. That is insufficient rather than merely inconvenient -- the claim this failure mode makes is specifically that the cache dict grows without bound, and resident memory cannot separate that from a workload change, a leak elsewhere, or allocator behaviour. No entry count is exported today, which is the gap mr-cache-entries-gauge closes, and that attribution is what turns an observation into a diagnosis.

payload_or_id.title: Process is killed for exhausting memory
payload_or_id.description: The unbounded cache eventually exhausts the process or container memory limit and the process is OOM-killed, taking every in-flight request with it. Total loss of service until restart, and restart clears the cache, so the system recovers fully and then walks the same path again on a period set by traffic -- a sawtooth that reads as an infrastructure flap rather than as a cache defect. The final link of the boundedness chain and the only one users perceive; every link above it is detectable hours or days earlier. Better served by implemented instrumentation than any other metric-gap mode here: process_resident_memory_bytes, auto-registered by prometheus_client, measures the exact quantity that causes the kill, and is a more direct signal than the recommended cache-entry gauge, which is a proxy requiring a bytes-per-entry ratio nobody has measured. It stays metric-gap on two grounds -- it is gated on exposition, and resident memory alone cannot attribute the growth to the cache, so it cannot distinguish this chain from an unrelated memory regression, which is the difference between paging someone and telling them what to fix.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics never reach a scraper
payload_or_id.description: Nothing in this repo exposes the default registry: no start_http_server, no ASGI or WSGI metrics app, no push gateway. Whatever exposes it lives outside this repo, unverified. If that path is absent, misconfigured, or the scrape target is wrong or down, everything the registry holds is written to memory and discarded -- not only the single Counter this codebase declares, but the process, platform and GC collectors prometheus_client auto-registers on import, which include process_resident_memory_bytes, the primary available signal for the OOM chain. The blast radius therefore covers both the instrumentation that still has to be written and the instrumentation that already exists for free. Critical, and first to confirm, because it is the common single point of failure beneath every alert in phases 3 and 4: a broken scrape path presents as a silent, permanently healthy-looking service, which is the same picture as a service with no traffic. Detecting it cannot rely on the service's own metrics and needs an external liveness signal.

payload_or_id.title: Storage has no index, so every operation costs time proportional to the whole store
payload_or_id.description: get linear-scans the whole file to resolve one key and put reads and rewrites all of it to change one key, so both cost O(total keys) in time and I/O. Cost rises with the size of the store rather than with traffic, meaning the system degrades on a timescale governed by data growth and gives no warning tied to load. Compounded by the write path: as the file grows, put's rewrite window widens, which widens the exposure to the torn-read and truncation failures.
